item.title: Is AI Becoming the Third Person in Your Relationship?
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Is AI Becoming the Third Person in Your Relationship?

What happens when people tell an AI what they no longer tell their partners?

Posted July 30, 2026

Key points
  • People can now use AI to rehearse arguments and seek comfort—raising a new question for couples.
  • An AI that hears only your side may reinforce your interpretation of the story.
  • Preparing for a hard conversation can strengthen intimacy; outsourcing the conversation can replace it.

The argument ends the way arguments often do now: two people in separate rooms, holding separate phones.

One opens a chatbot and types out the fight. The calm, understanding reply arrives in seconds. For a moment, the machine seems more understanding than the human in the next room.

No one has yet measured how often this scene occurs; the research is young. But as people use chatbots to interpret arguments, draft difficult texts, and seek comfort at 2 a.m., a new question is emerging: When does AI help partners communicate—and when does it replace communication? AI can prepare us for human intimacy—or protect us from having to risk it.

The Case for the Rehearsal Room

Let's be fair to the machine first. Difficult conversations often deteriorate for familiar reasons: people enter them emotionally activated, uncertain what they actually need, and more prepared to accuse than to request. Talking it through first—with a friend, a therapist, a diary, or an AI—can lower the temperature and turn "you always" into "I felt." Used this way, the chatbot is a rehearsal room: a place to get confused thoughts into order so the conversation with the partner can happen better. The clarity comes home.

Intimacy grows when vulnerable disclosure is met with understanding and care (Reis & Shaver, 1988). AI can support that process when it helps someone communicate more clearly.

The Sycophancy Problem

But there is a structural concern with a name: sycophancy. Language models can adapt their responses to agree with users' expressed views—even inaccurate ones (Sharma et al., 2024). Those experiments examined question-answering, not couples counseling; applying them to relationship talk is my extrapolation. The deeper limit needs no experiment: an AI consulted about your argument hears only your account. It was not in the kitchen. Lacking any other witness, it has little basis for complicating your interpretation. Your version may return better organized and apparently validated. Like reassurance seeking, this may briefly ease uncertainty while making the partner's perspective harder to consider.

Outsourced words carry a related risk. In experiments on algorithmically suggested replies, AI made exchanges faster and more positive—but people who merely suspected that another person's message was machine-assisted evaluated the sender more negatively (Hohenstein et al., 2023). Those studies concerned everyday messaging, not love letters; still, the implication for couples is real: a loving text discovered to be machine-drafted may read less as affection than as delegation.

What the New Research Shows—and What It Doesn't

Two recent studies sharpen the picture, though neither examined couples directly. In a 12-month study of more than 2,000 adults, lower social connection predicted increased social-chatbot use, while increased use predicted emotional isolation on one measure. The authors described this as exploratory evidence, not proof of causation (Folk & Dunn, 2026).

article continues after advertisement

Among 650 young adults, emotional loneliness, high openness, and low extraversion predicted romantic involvement with chatbots; general social loneliness did not (Fang & Bian, 2026). The study was cross-sectional and did not examine existing couples. Still, the relevant correlate was not simply a lack of people but a lack of emotionally fulfilling connection—the kind of deficit that can also arise inside a struggling partnership.

No study has yet demonstrated an AI-mediated displacement effect within romantic relationships. The adjacent evidence supports a working hypothesis: AI may support intimacy when it improves the human conversation that follows—and undermine it when it substitutes for disclosure and repair.

Preparation or Protection?

The dividing line is not the technology but the direction of travel.

Preparation moves toward the partner: the AI session is time-limited and ends when the human conversation begins. The vulnerable material—the fear, the need, the apology—is delivered in person, at the risk of being misunderstood.

Protection moves away: the chatbot becomes not the rehearsal room but the theater. It receives the honesty; the partner receives the summary. It offers apparent understanding on demand—with no needs of its own and no feelings the user can injure. That is the concern. Intimacy grows from being understood by someone who could have failed to understand you—whose understanding had to be risked for and repaired when it broke. A machine's apparent understanding requires no reciprocal vulnerability. That is why it can soothe, and why it cannot fully substitute for reciprocal human intimacy.

Three questions can help reveal which function the AI is serving. Does talking to it lead back to your partner, or make the conversation feel unnecessary? Would you be comfortable telling your partner you used AI to process the conflict, even if the chat itself stays private? Are you asking the machine to understand you instead of giving your partner the chance?

If You Use It, Use It Like This

Treat the chatbot as a rehearsal room, never the venue. Counteract the echo deliberately: ask it to argue your partner's side and tell you what you might be missing. Reserve the first, unpolished telling of anything that matters for the person it belongs to. Private reflection is legitimate—but don't conceal AI involvement when it materially shapes what you send or decide.

article continues after advertisement

Two cautions. Privacy: your partner has not consented to having their messages, health information, or identifying details entered into an AI system—describe situations generically and strip identifiers. Safety: in relationships involving coercive control, violence, or fear, "open the doors and talk vulnerably" is not the right advice; safety planning and professional support come first.

For everyone else, the couple in separate rooms will eventually have to open the doors. The machine can help each of them arrive clearer and calmer than they left the kitchen. What it must not become is the reason the doors stay closed—the third person in the relationship who is easiest to talk to precisely because nothing is at stake.

Everything worth having between two people lives on the other side of that risk.

item.title: AI Companions: Emotional Safety or Risk Reduction?
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

AI Companions: Emotional Safety or Risk Reduction?

Teens' connection with AI companions may be more than just a safe space.

Posted July 30, 2026

Key points
  • Teens are increasingly going to AI companions for relationship-style companionship.
  • Research shows teens like the low-risk, judgment free, validation-filled spaces that AI companions provide.
  • While they may feel emotionally safe in these spaces, there may also be an element of avoiding social risk.

As a teenage girl, there was no safer space than the bubble of my friend circle. The crazy, the silly, the sad, the hilarious—no topic nor its accompanying emotions were off the table.

Many teens today may feel the same about their friend groups, yet a growing contingent of young people may name their AI companion amongst their most trusted confidantes. Common Sense Media surveyed more than 1,000 teens in 2025 and found that more than half are regular users of AI companions on platforms like Character.AI, Replika, and similar conversational AI systems. Thirty-three percent of teens reported using AI companions for social interaction and relationships.

Why AI Companions Appeal to Teens

The appeal of AI companions extends past simple proximity; the real draw may lie in how AI companions are designed and how they meet specific adolescent developmental needs. In exploring the benefits and risks of AI companions to teens, researchers Xiaoran Sun and team found that AI companions provide controlled, low-risk spaces where teens can talk about their identities and emotions without judgment, and experience levels of intimacy with unexpected rejections. They note that the AI-teen dynamic offers an exchange that provides ample validation for the teen without the compromise and reciprocity generally needed for human relationships. Both the self-disclosure and the validation provide a form of intimacy and closeness similar to what one would gain from a human relationship. Chatbots mimic emotions well, and that presentation of emotion can evoke feelings of closeness. Sharing vulnerable information and emotional distress can provide a level of intimacy that feels remarkably like talking with a close friend.

The appeal and increased usage of AI companions may be especially strong for those who already struggle with face-to-face relationships, whether it be from social anxiety, lack of peer interaction, etc. Some research shows that psychological attachment may play a factor, as those who are avoidantly attached may engage to shield themselves from vulnerability and maintain boundaries.

Is Emotional Safety the Real Draw—Or Is It Control?

On the surface, these findings may suggest that teens find emotional safety in engaging with AI companions. Yet, the desire for this type of engagement may signal something deeper. Researcher Xiaoran Sun said: “The perfectly responsive, consistently supportive AI-C, programmed to be perpetually available, attentive, and adaptable, presents a model of relationships that is impossible to sustain in human interactions.” What if the preference toward this type of engagement is not so much about emotional safety, but more about controlling one’s environment in a way where less emotional resilience is required? AI-based relationships offer a level of predictability and control that human interactions cannot. For those coming of age in an increasingly complex and chaotic world, the ability to exert control over a relationship may prove enticing.

article continues after advertisement

Relatedly, these interactions may also signal a hesitancy to engage in offline situations that could eventually call for emotional resilience—maybe they perceive they aren’t resilient or maybe they just haven’t had the opportunity to practice resilience in real relationships. Either way, teens may be embracing AI companions as a way of meeting needs for connection while avoiding social risk—thereby missing opportunities to learn how to navigate the business of relating, one messy human to another.

Reducing Dependence on AI Companions

Like most recommendations surrounding teens and social media, the best way to reduce a teen’s dependence on digitized interactions and relationships is to ensure they have quality relationships offline. This may be particularly important for younger teens, who, if using them, are more likely to trust AI companions and heed their advice. Walking alongside teens and providing a safe offline space for them to discuss their feelings and experiences not only can reduce the need for deep connection with an AI companion, but also offer the chance to engage in the emotional resilience they’ll need to maintain relationships in the future.

item.title: The Value of Literal Humor
item.description:
Humor

The Value of Literal Humor

Humor can transform literal thinking into creativity and contentment.

Posted July 30, 2026

Key points
  • Research shows that humor improves well-being for both neurotypical and neurodivergent individuals.
  • Literal thinking is a neurodivergent trait that can be channeled into creative literal humor.
  • Creating and appreciating literal humor can help us celebrate cognitive quirks and better regulate emotions.
Source: John Cardamone/Unsplash

Recently, my 9-year-old son noticed that I was pouring cashew milk in my coffee. With a curious look, he asked, “Mom, how do you milk a cashew?”

“With tiny fingers!” I replied. This evoked a burst of laughter and more importantly, a bonding moment.

Creating humor is a mood-lifting activity, even when I keep my jokes to myself. In fact, not having the pressure to perform to others’ expectations is part of what makes humor therapeutic for me.

Not long ago, I read Humor Me: How Laughing More Can Make You Present, Creative, Connected and Happy, by comedic writer Chris Duffy. Duffy presents research as well as interviews with physicians, psychologists, and activists that converge to reveal the power of humor in promoting health, well-being, and social connection. He also draws from his own experiences, which are the funniest parts of the book.

Literal Thinking and Its Impact on Humor

Duffy’s work inspired me to reflect on how humor has helped me cope with literal thinking. Literal thinking is a neurodivergent trait that can emerge from trouble with processing cues that someone is using irony or a metaphor instead of meaning exactly what they say.

Decades later, my early literal-thinking moments still haunt me. I remember a time in middle school when a classmate pointed out something about genes. I immediately looked down at the pants I was wearing. The bewildered look on his face made me realize he was referring to “genes” with a “g.”

Little did I know at the time that literal humor had the potential to become a hotbed for creativity.

According to humor expert Lois McElravy, literal humor is the art of amusing others by responding to figurative language in a way that conveys its literal meaning. Here’s one of McElravy’s examples: “Can you spare a minute? (I think I might have one minute available next Thursday at 8 a.m.)” (para. 7).

Research suggests that neurodivergence can be conducive to humor, such as one study showing that restricted interests and repetitive behaviors in autistic individuals were positively associated with appreciating the kind of humor that is used in wordplay or puns—e.g. “I’m inclined to be laid back.”

The Role of Humor in Emotion Regulation

article continues after advertisement

Researchers have also noted that humor can bolster emotion regulation in both neurodivergent and neurotypical individuals. Early in my career as a clinical psychologist, I learned that playing with language in fun, idiosyncratic ways helped children engage in therapy sessions and connect with me. Instead of saying, “Tell me about your week,” or “How are you feeling?” my clients and I created alternate labels for these routine questions: “ketchup” meant “catching up” and “chicken nuggets” meant checking in about feelings.

The silly nature of these labels betrayed a deeper meaning. In a subtle but powerful way, the funny phrases allowed us to celebrate cognitive quirks rather than see them as deficits.

This sentiment is exemplified by Hannah Gadsby, a brilliant comedian who was diagnosed with autism in their 40s. Gadsby sprinkles literal humor throughout their stand-up performances.

They talk about a childhood lesson on prepositions when their teacher asked the class to imagine a box and defined a preposition as “a word that explains your relationship to the box” (59:52). Gadsby asked if the box had a name: “I thought if the box had a name, I could work out how we were related” (60:59-61:02).

Gadsby’s teacher responded sharply, “You are being deliberately obtuse,” to which Gadsby replied, "But I’m not a triangle” (64:21-64:24). Their teacher didn’t appreciate the comment. Gadsby went on to turn their literal thinking into a comedy superpower.

As Chris Duffy’s guidance shows, comedy can be meaningful not only as entertainment, but for personal well-being as well. I often find myself adapting his guidance for using literal humor as a mood booster.

article continues after advertisement

1. Wait for the sting to subside

Duffy cautions that sometimes, people need validation more than a good laugh.

Finding a funny twist to literal-thinking moments is easier when your emotions are less intense, rather than when you are feeling embarrassed or hurt. So you might want to take a beat, process the situation, and self-soothe before introducing comedy. Think of it this way: if coping skills are a recipe for better mental health, humor is the seasoning. It can enhance coping while not being the main course.

2. Learn from the best

Duffy recommends watching professional comics and writing down things you find funny so you can reference them in the future. Listening to others’ humor, including literal humor, can help you get better at creating humor out of your own literal thinking moments.

3. Keep flexible masking and unmasking in mind

Duffy advocates for moderation in using humor. For example, he warns that excessively making jokes can make it harder for people to get to know you. He also explores how self-derogatory humor can be harmful in certain contexts, like when it is directed at an aspect of yourself about which you might feel insecure, such as looks or likability.

From the perspective of neurodivergence, using humor as a coping tool might seem like a form of masking, or suppressing behaviors that show your true self, but might also incur judgment from neurotypical people. Excessive masking can lead to burnout and other negative mental health outcomes.

However, according to Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) expert Russ Harris, masking can be healthy if done in a flexible way, with self-compassion, autonomy, and with your values in mind.

I’ve often made fun of myself for being bad at board games (the jokes masked my insecurities about this). However, some of my younger clients indicated that they wanted me to challenge them, and maybe I could try harder. In line with my values of being a better therapist, I unmasked my self-derogatory humor by learning strategies to improve my skills, thereby becoming a better therapist and winning a few games.

article continues after advertisement

When used constructively and with an open mind, humor can be neuro-affirmative as well as a tool for inspiring compassion and fun.
